title: Python Standard Library Quick Revision: re, datetime, logging, json, collections, itertools, argparse
summary: Night-before revision notes for the Python stdlib modules used most in everyday scripts and interviews: regex patterns and groups, timezone-aware datetimes with zoneinfo, logging configuration, JSON, collections, itertools and argparse.

chapters.title: Stdlib Toolkit: Mental Model and Regex Patterns
points: re.search scans anywhere, re.match anchors at the start only, re.fullmatch must match the whole string; each returns a Match object or None, so check before calling .group()
Core tokens: \d digit, \w word char, \s whitespace, . any char except newline, ^ and $ anchors, [abc] class, a|b alternation
Quantifiers * + ? {n,m} are greedy by default; add ? (like .*?) for lazy matching, e.g. re.findall(r'<.+?>', '<a><b>') returns ['<a>', '<b>']
Always use raw strings r'\d+' for patterns, since '\b' in a normal string is a backspace character, not a word boundary
re.compile(p) pre-builds a reusable pattern object, and flags like re.I, re.M, re.S, re.X go in as the second argument

chapters.title: Regex Groups and Substitution
points: Parentheses (...) capture; m.group(0) is the full match, m.group(1) the first group, m.groups() a tuple of all groups
Named groups (?P<year>\d{4}) are read with m.group('year') or m.groupdict(), which is safer than numeric indexes
(?:...) is a non-capturing group: it groups for quantifiers or alternation without adding a numbered group
re.findall returns a list of strings, or a list of tuples when the pattern has 2+ groups; re.finditer yields Match objects with positions via .span()
re.sub(pattern, repl, s) replaces matches, reuses groups with \1 or \g<name>, and accepts a function as repl; an unmatched optional group returns None

chapters.title: datetime, Timezones and zoneinfo
points: Naive datetime has tzinfo=None and an aware one carries a timezone; comparing or subtracting naive with aware raises TypeError

Create aware times with datetime.now(ZoneInfo('Asia/Kolkata')) or datetime(2026,3,8,tzinfo=ZoneInfo('UTC')); datetime.utcnow() is deprecated and returns a naive value, so use datetime.now(timezone.utc)
Convert between zones with dt.astimezone(ZoneInfo('America/New_York')); the instant stays the same and only the display changes
Pass tzinfo=ZoneInfo(...) to the constructor instead of pytz-style localize; zoneinfo handles DST via the tz database (install the tzdata package on Windows)

Format with strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S%z') and parse with strptime(s, fmt) or datetime.fromisoformat(s); timedelta does arithmetic, e.g. dt + timedelta(days=1), and store UTC, convert only for display

chapters.title: Logging Configuration and JSON
points: Levels in order: DEBUG 10, INFO 20, WARNING 30, ERROR 40, CRITICAL 50; the default root level is WARNING, so logging.info prints nothing until configured
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format='%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s') sets up the root handler, and only the first call has any effect
Use one logger per module with log = logging.getLogger(__name__); a logger's level filters first, then each handler's level filters again, and records propagate up to the parent's handlers
Log lazily with log.info('user %s', uid) instead of f-strings, and use log.exception('failed') inside except to include the traceback; add handlers like FileHandler or RotatingFileHandler for output

json.dumps(obj, indent=2) and json.loads(s) work on strings, while json.dump and json.load work on file objects; sort_keys=True gives stable output, and non-serializable types such as datetime or set need default=str or a custom encoder; JSON turns tuples into lists and int dict keys into strings

chapters.title: collections and itertools
points: Counter(iterable) counts hashables, and .most_common(n) returns the top n as (item, count) pairs; missing keys return 0 instead of raising KeyError, and counters support + and - arithmetic
defaultdict(list) creates a missing key's value from the factory on first access, which is ideal for grouping; merely reading a missing key inserts it, so use .get() to avoid that
deque(maxlen=n) gives O(1) append and popleft at both ends and auto-discards old items, unlike list.pop(0) which is O(n); it has no efficient middle indexing

itertools.chain(a, b) joins iterables, islice(it, n) slices any iterator, groupby(data, key) groups only consecutive items so sort first, and product/permutations/combinations(it, r) generate combinatorics lazily

itertools functions return one-shot iterators that are exhausted after one pass, so wrap them in list() if you need to reuse the results; accumulate gives running totals and zip_longest pads uneven inputs

chapters.title: argparse and Stdlib Cheat Sheet
points: Pattern: p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=...); p.add_argument(...); args = p.parse_args(); positional args are required, while --flag options are optional by default
add_argument options: type=int, default=, choices=[...], required=True, help=, nargs='+' for one or more values, dest= for the attribute name
Boolean flags use action='store_true'; action='count' for -vvv and action='append' for repeated options; --dry-run is read as args.dry_run
Subcommands use p.add_subparsers(dest='cmd'), then sp.add_parser('run'); -h is generated for free and bad input exits with code 2

One-line recall: re.fullmatch/named groups, datetime.now(ZoneInfo(...)), getLogger(__name__), json.dumps/loads, Counter.most_common, defaultdict(list), deque(maxlen), groupby after sort, argparse parse_args
